summary: The article describes a revival of home canning and fermenting of seasonal produce in autumn 2023, driven by interest in sustainability and self-sufficiency. It covers the basic science of each method, quotes practitioners and experts, and notes the community clubs, safety concerns, environmental benefits and health and heritage value of preserving food.
one_line: Home canning and fermenting of seasonal foods is reviving in autumn 2023, driven by sustainability, community, health and heritage, with expert safety advice.
key_facts: Susan Meyers, a master canner, has been leading canning workshops since spring 2023 and learned from her grandmother's pantry of homemade jams, pickles and sauces.
Canning works by placing food in jars and heating them to destroy spoilage microorganisms; properly sealed jars keep out air and bacteria.
Tomatoes, beans, cucumbers, peaches and berries are named as common raw materials for canning, used for sauces, chutneys and jams.
Emily Wilson, a food blogger, documented her canning journey and describes making peach preserves that carry the memory of summer.
Fermented foods such as sauerkraut, kimchi and kefir are valued for probiotic qualities that aid digestion and gut health.
Fermentation converts carbohydrates to alcohol or organic acids using yeasts or bacteria under anaerobic conditions.
Max Hart, owner of Hart's Ferments, started his local fermentation business on November 1, 2023, and compares fermentation to alchemy.
Food scientist Dr. Lisa Nguyen led a seminar on safe canning practices on September 15, 2023, and urged following tested recipes because botulism from improper canning is rare but a real risk.
The Happy Valley Preservers, founded by Roberto Garcia, formed on September 22, 2023, meet bi-weekly and have seen a membership spike.
Environmental activist Jane Lee spoke at a sustainable food conference on October 10, 2023, saying preserving food reduces waste and supports local agriculture.
Canning and fermenting reduce reliance on out-of-season imports that are picked before ripening and shipped long distances.
Home-canned and fermented foods can be free of the additives and preservatives common in store-bought versions.
